transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-10 15:00 PST · 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SRE); Aisha Khan (Cobalt Platform Eng), Mark Liu (Cobalt SRE), Nora Feld (Head of ML), Ben Ortiz (Security)

Summary: Quick technical deep dive on geo backpressure and fallback policies, how to warm/prime KV cache across regions, and playbook steps for DR + runbook tabletop. Benchmarks and scripts to follow.

Topics: geo-backpressure mechanics, prefix/KV priming, cross-region warmup, batching behavior during failback, quantization tradeoffs for cold starts, VPC egress considerations, DR tabletop cadence

Action items (see metadata)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): ok thanks everyone for jumping on; main goal today is to align on a fallback/backpressure strategy when regional capacity is constrained and to cover KV priming so cold starts don't kill latency.
[00:22] Aisha (Cobalt): thanks, yes, we've been seeing spikes in EU-west and the fallback has been somewhat noisy — requests go to US sometimes and latency doubles. want to avoid token storms.
[00:35] Samira (Redwood SE): totally. we'll talk about policy-first routing, circuit breakers, and also a light-weight KV priming approach so that when you redirect traffic you don't pay full cold-start.
[00:47] Mark (Cobalt SRE): quick note: our VPC has strict egress rules to certain regions; we need to map that before any automated failover.
[00:56] Diego (Redwood SRE): noted — we'll need a mapped table of allowed endpoints per region. can also support a manual approve for the first run.
[01:10] Nora (Head of ML): curious on quantization impact — we saw int8 models save cost but warmups seemed longer. is that expected?
[01:22] Samira: short answer: int8 can increase initial kernel selection time because of dequant/scatter paths, but once warmed KV and the kernels are resident it's faster and cheaper. the nuance is prefix-KV warmup: if you only prime the KV cache with typical prefixes you avoid most heavy compute on redirect.
[01:45] Jordan: i'll share an example priming script — it's basically a batched replay of top 500 prompt prefixes over the last 24h with controlled qps throttling.
[02:02] Aisha: do you recommend priming all regions or just neighbor regions? our budget is limited.
[02:10] Samira: prioritize: 1) target DR regions you plan to fail to (hot standby), 2) second-tier cold replicas with partial priming (top 50 prompts), 3) do not blanket-prime across all zones unless you have reserved capacity. the playbook includes a cost model.
[02:31] [02:31] Ben (Security): from compliance, we need audit logs of the failover event and list of models and versions used. can we get that exported?
[02:40] Diego: yes — all rollouts/fallbacks create a run entry in the control plane with model version, kernel profile, batch settings, and a unique event id. logs can be routed to your SIEM via our log forwarder.
[02:53] Mark: perfect. also what about sticky sessions? some of our calls are conversational and client state shouldn't bounce around mid-dialog.
[03:05] Samira: we support sticky routing per conversation id; policy can be set to stick for X minutes and optionally evict on error. fallback policy can be configured to only move new requests, not ongoing conversations, unless manual override.
[03:23] Nora: pretend we lose EU-west; what's the step-by-step?
[03:30] Jordan: quick runbook sketch:
- detection: autoscaler/uptime monitors + increased error rate triggers;
- mitigation: apply pre-configured region-backpressure that reduces QPS to degraded pool and triggers failover to hot standby region (policy-based);
- priming: run warmup job against hot standby if not primed; we do a staged priming: quick top-50 prefixes at 10rps then expand;
- traffic shift: weighted routing over 3 stages (10/30/60) with health-check gating;
- rollback: automatic rollback if error budget exceeded or manual abort.
[04:05] Aisha: that weighted approach seems sensible. how do you throttle priming so it doesn't starve the live region?
[04:12] Samira: priming runs at low priority and uses isolated capacity when possible; we recommend priming from a separate warmup pool or using reserved burst capacity. also continuous-batching helps — priming payloads are batched to maximize GPU throughput with minimal per-token penalty.
[04:35] [04:35] Mark: about KV segmentation — do you shard the KV by customer or by prefix namespace? we want to avoid cross-tenant noise.
[04:45] Diego: Redwood stores KV per-customer namespace by default; cross-region replication is asynchronous. for failover we do a metadata-first check: if KV lag > threshold we either run prefix priming or fallback to model-variant that is less KV-dependent (e.g., stateless or smaller prefix reliance).
[05:10] Ben: does that mean some fallbacks will return slightly lower quality? what is the rollback SLA on quality?
[05:18] Samira: yes, quality vs latency is a tradeoff. in the console you can configure quality SLOs tied to prompt-sets; if fallback reduces quality below threshold we either increase latency budget or route to a different region. we also support A/B style routing to measure degradation.
[05:39] Nora: related: when priming across regions, do you copy full KV or just top hot keys? copy cost is concerning.
[05:48] Samira: only hot keys recommended. our priming script supports ranked prefix lists; you can prime top-N and monitor latency benefit. full copy is possible but expensive; for large corpora we suggest a hybrid: metadata + targeted priming.
[06:05] Jordan: i'll attach the template ranking file — it's a csv of prefix, weight, freq.
[06:13] [06:13] Aisha: let's talk observability — we need token-level breakdown and per-route p50/p95 across regions to validate the shift.
[06:22] Diego: console exposes per-route token cost, average batch size, and kernel selection histograms. we also provide a tracing hook for end-to-end request ids so you can stitch backend timing.
[06:37] Mark: can we get alerts if kernel selection changes significantly after a failover? those changes often explain latency regressions.
[06:44] Samira: yes — you can set a regression alert based on kernel profile delta or p95 increase. we'll send a sample dashboard JSON with recommended alerts.
[06:57] [07:00] (noise)
[07:13] Nora: question on continuous batching: during periods of sudden redirect traffic, does batching increase latency variance?
[07:21] Samira: short: potential for slight variance at very low QPS, but overall batching improves throughput and reduces per-token cost. the routing layer can keep a small per-request timeout budget to avoid holding tokens too long. Also we do adaptive batching: at low QPS we favor latency (smaller batch), at high QPS we increase batch window.
[07:45] Aisha: that makes sense. what about model quantization knobs for faster cold starts?
[07:52] Diego: some knobs: 1) keep model in fp16 for faster kernel warmup, 2) maintain a light-weight int8 fallback for throughput once warmed, 3) use model-snapshotting to preserve kernel cache between restarts. each has tradeoffs in memory and accuracy.
[08:12] Ben: snapshotting sounds good, is it compatible with air-gapped on-prem deployments?
[08:18] Diego: yes — snapshots are just binary artifacts you can pull into your on-prem runtime. for VPC/on-prem we provide an offline priming tool so you can pre-warm without external egress.
[08:29] Jordan: quick demo note: we'll include a short recording of a priming run showing p95 drop from 1.2s to 220ms after priming in the EU->US failover test.
[08:40] Aisha: what about bursty token patterns (long tails) — will priming still help?
[08:46] Samira: yes for prefix-heavy workloads; for highly unpredictable tails priming has diminishing returns. that's where quality-based routing and model selection matters: we can route tail-heavy prompts to a variant with larger context or more compute but higher latency budget.
[09:05] Nora: can Redwood simulate region loss and run a tabletop? we want to test our SACM and runbook.
[09:12] Jordan: yes. propose a 60-min DR tabletop: scenario simulate EU-west outage, runbook execution, priming steps, and rollback. Redwood will act as facilitator and produce a playbook after.
[09:24] Mark: include SRE + infra + security. and please include the VPC peering checklist.
[09:30] Ben: security question: when you prime with customer data, is any of that persisted outside the customer namespace or logs? we have PII concerns.
[09:40] Diego: we keep priming requests in customer namespace, and control plane only stores metadata (prefix hashes, counts). raw prompts flagged sensitive are redacted in logs by default; we can switch to no retention mode for the priming run.
[09:55] Aisha: good, send docs.
[10:00] Jordan: we'll send security docs and the playbook draft. also a short script that replays prefixes into a region with built-in QPS throttle and batch grouping.
[10:12] [10:12] Samira: a few implementation specifics to call out: 1) when failing over, we prefer weighted gradual shift to avoid request storms, 2) circuit breaker thresholds are token-rate and error-rate based, 3) fallback model-variants can be configured inline by tag, so easy to switch to less KV reliant models, 4) priming scripts respect privacy modes and avoid logging raw prompts.
[10:41] Nora: any suggested quantization profile for long context models?
[10:45] Samira: for long-context we suggest mixed-precision: keep attention and KV compute in fp16, quantize matmul-heavy layers to int8. that preserves context handling while reducing memory. we'll share a recommended profile matrix.
[10:59] Jordan: shipping note: we'll attach two artifacts — priming script + benchmark sheet, playbook draft, and the dashboard JSON.
[11:08] Aisha: timeline — can you get the priming script today and the benchmark results next week?
[11:14] Jordan: yes — script today, results after Samira runs the quick sim.
[11:18] Mark: final: define SLAs for failover window — how long until traffic is fully shifted?
[11:25] Samira: default safe window is 15 minutes for gradual shift, but with reserved burst can be reduced to ~3-5 minutes; tradeoff is increased cost. we'll include options in the playbook.
[11:38] Nora: thanks — would like one pager on cost vs time tradeoffs.
[11:42] Jordan: will include.
[11:45] (end)
